source.title: Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches to Athletes’ Preparation: A Review

paper.citation: Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. Sports Medicine, 46(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5
paper.abstract: What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation? The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies. It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football. Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models. The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis. Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.
paper.tldr: This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing. Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models. The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis. Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.
paper.findings: Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities.
paper.limitations: Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis. Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history. Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football. The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
